new_statements.quote: In all of the Chapacuran languages for which audio recordings or reliable transcriptions are available, sentential stress occurs on the final syllable of the predicating element, before the verbal inflection (Everett & Kern 1997, Leigue Castedo 1957, Nimuendajú 1925, Weinold 2012).2 When a predicate is composed of multiple verbs forming a serial verb construction, the primary stress occurs on the final syllable of the final verb. [fn. 2:] Multisyllablic words generally receive primary lexical stress on the final syllable, e.g. [poˌɾo.naˈkon] 'his bow' in Oro Win. See Birchall (to appear) for further discussion on stress and intonation in Chapacuran languages.
new_statements.citation: Birchall, Joshua. 2018. Historical change in reported speech constructions in the Chapacuran family. Journal of Historical Linguistics 8(1): 7-30. doi:10.1075/jhl.00003.bir.

new_statements.relation_note: Family-level final stress (word and sentence); nothing on tone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Across Chapacuran (evidence base explicitly including Nimuendajú's 1925 Torá transcriptions), primary lexical stress falls on the final syllable of multisyllabic words; at sentence level the main stress falls on the final syllable of the predicating element (the last verb of a serial construction), immediately before the unstressed inflectional particle.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; the one transcribed example [poˌɾo.naˈkon] (Oro Win) shows a secondary stress two syllables before the final primary.
new_statements.exceptions: 'generally' (no list of exceptions); post-verbal inflectional particles are unstressed; a verbal modifier standing between predicate and particle takes the sentential stress instead of the verb (sect. 2, exx. 13-14, Oro Win).
new_statements.identity_note: Family-wide paper by the Chapacuran specialist; Torá (Moreic branch, Nimuendajú 1925 data) is one of the languages exemplified (exx. 4, 6, 9, 26, all from Nimuendajú 1925: 154-157). The stress statement is a generalisation over 'all of the Chapacuran languages for which audio recordings or reliable transcriptions are available' and explicitly lists Nimuendajú 1925 - the Torá source - among its evidence; it is therefore second-hand for Torá (read off Nimuendajú's accent marks), first-hand for Oro Win/Wari'/Moré.

new_statements.quote: O fator demarcativo do lexema é, portanto, o peso silábico, uma vez que uma sílaba pesada caracteriza sempre o final de um lexema, ao passo que uma sílaba leve caracteriza sempre a primeira sílaba de um lexema dissílabo. [...] Nas línguas Chapakura, a acentuação dos lexemas é dedutível do peso silábico - o único fator prosódico fonológico nessa família lingüística. Portanto, o acento não é fonológico por ser previsível. [...] A atualização fonética da acentuação lexical obedece às seguintes regras: (a) uma sílaba leve é átona e possui um tom baixo. [...] (b) uma sílaba pesada é tônica e possui um tom alto. [followed by the rule / # (σ) σ # / → [ (σ̀) »σ́ ]]
new_statements.translation: The demarcating factor of the lexeme is therefore syllable weight, since a heavy syllable always characterizes the end of a lexeme, whereas a light syllable always characterizes the first syllable of a disyllabic lexeme. [...] In the Chapakura languages the accentuation of lexemes is deducible from syllable weight - the only phonological prosodic factor in this family. Stress is therefore not phonological, being predictable. [...] The phonetic realization of lexical accentuation obeys the following rules: (a) a light syllable is unstressed and has low pitch [...] (b) a heavy syllable is stressed and has high pitch. [rule: /#(σ)σ#/ → [(σ̀)ˈσ́]]

No Tora-specific prosodic statement; net effect of the family rule (heavy syllable always lexeme-final and stressed) is final stress. | checker: File…
new_statements.relation_note: Explicit predictable final (heavy-syllable) stress with high pitch as co-exponent; no lexical tone ('o peso silábico - o único fator prosódico fonológico').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide (all Chapakura languages, Torá included by the author): every lexeme is a monosyllable (one heavy syllable) or a disyllable (light + heavy); the heavy syllable is always lexeme-final and always carries the stress (strong intensity) and high pitch, the light first syllable is unstressed and low; stress is predictable from weight, hence non-contrastive. Net effect: stress on the final syllable of every lexeme/word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none described (lexemes are at most disyllabic; in casual registers up to three lexemes may fuse into one phonological word, each heavy syllable keeping its prominence)
new_statements.exceptions: None for the rule itself; ch. 5 / the 2000 paper report diachronic weakening of the prominence ('plateaux', 'modalidade frágil') in Oro Win and a pitch shift to the light first syllable in Oro Mon, while intensity stays on the heavy final syllable everywhere.

The stress rule itself was measured acoustically on five living languages (Miguelenho, Moré, Kuyubi, Oro Mon, Oro Win; ch. 5) and is asserted family-wide; for Torá the author applies it herself: 96 Torá cognate entries in sect. 4.4 (pp. 67-119) are phonologized and given phonetic forms with the stress mark [»] on the final (heavy) syllable, e.g. tor /ʔimin/ [ʔɪ̆»mín] 'anta', /ʔupik/ [ʔʊ̆»pík̚], /ʔoRom/ [ʔŏ»Róbm] 'cuia', /ʔawin/ [ʔă»wídn], monosyllables [»káw] 'comer', [»tíbm] 'coração'. new_statements.translation: The demarcating factor of the lexeme is therefore syllable weight, since a heavy syllable always marks the end of a lexeme while a light syllable always marks the first syllable of a disyllabic lexeme. [...] In the Chapakura languages the accentuation of lexemes is deducible from syllable weight - the only prosodic factor with a phonological role in this family. new_statements.rule_in_words: In all Chapakura languages lexemes are (light+)heavy; the heavy syllable is always final and carries predictable, non-contrastive stress (intensity + high pitch); i.e. lexeme-final stress family-wide. Torá not individually discussed.

new_statements.quote: Nas línguas Chapakura, a acentuação dos lexemas é dedutível do peso silábico - o único fator prosódico fonológico nessa família lingüística. Portanto, o acento não é fonológico por ser previsível. [...] A atualização fonética da acentuação lexical obedece às seguintes regras: (a) uma sílaba leve é átona e possui um tom baixo. Em outras palavras, carrega um acento de intensidade (“stress”) fraco e um acento de altura (“pitch”) baixo; (b) uma sílaba pesada é tônica e possui um tom alto. Em outras palavras, carrega um acento de intensidade (“stress”) forte e um acento de altura (“pitch”) alto. [p.22:] O fator demarcativo do lexema é, portanto, o peso silábico, uma vez que uma sílaba pesada caracteriza sempre o final de um lexema, ao passo que uma sílaba leve caracteriza sempre a primeira sílaba de um lexema dissílabo.
new_statements.translation: In the Chapakura languages, the accentuation of lexemes is deducible from syllable weight - the only phonological prosodic factor in this language family. Stress is therefore not phonological, being predictable. [...] The phonetic realization of lexical accentuation obeys the following rules: (a) a light syllable is unstressed and has a low tone, i.e. it carries weak intensity accent ('stress') and low pitch accent; (b) a heavy syllable is stressed and has a high tone, i.e. it carries strong 'stress' and high 'pitch'. [p.22:] The demarcative factor of the lexeme is therefore syllable weight, since a heavy syllable always characterizes the end of a lexeme, whereas a light syllable always characterizes the first syllable of a disyllabic lexeme.

new_statements.relation_note: Family-level statement: Chapakura lexical stress is non-contrastive and deducible from syllable weight; light syllable = unstressed, low pitch; heavy syllable = stressed, high pitch; heavy syllable is obligatorily lexeme-final (sect. 2.1.1-2.2, pp.21-23; restated sect. 4.2.2 p.68; Anexo pp.146-149 on acoustic correlates and per-language evolution in Moré, Oro Win etc.). Pitch is described as a redundant correlate of stress/weight, not lexical tone. Torá itself gets only a segmental section (3.11, pp.58-60, phonemes and phonotactics from Nimuendajú 1925) with no Torá-specific stress remark. Text of sect. 2.2 is identical to the etnolinguistica copy of the 1997 dissertation (work 1; there at…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lexemes are monosyllabic (one heavy syllable CVC/CV:/CVV) or disyllabic (light CV + heavy); stress (with redundant high pitch) falls on the heavy syllable, which is always lexeme-final, so every lexeme is stressed on its final syllable; the author treats weight as primary and stress as predictable/non-phonemic. Schema p.23: /#(σ)σ#/ -> [(σ̀) ˈσ́]. Sect. 4.2.2 (p.68) projects the same system onto Proto-Chapakura 'em função do comportamento homogêneo das diversas línguas Chapakura'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not discussed (light syllable simply 'átona', weak stress, low pitch)
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement; casual/hypoarticulated registers allow vowel shortening and fusion of monosyllabic lexemes (rule (2), p.22-23), which affects phonological-word count, not the heavy=stressed rule.

sources.note: Family-level statement: Chapakura lexical stress is non-contrastive and deducible from syllable weight; light syllable = unstressed, low pitch; heavy syllable = stressed, high pitch; heavy syllable is obligatorily lexeme-final (sect. 2.1.1-2.2, pp.21-23; restated sect. 4.2.2 p.68; Anexo pp.146-149 on acoustic correlates and per-language evolution in Moré, Oro Win etc.). Pitch is described as a redundant correlate of stress/weight, not lexical tone. Torá itself gets only a segmental section (3.11, pp.58-60, phonemes and phonotactics from Nimuendajú 1925) with no Torá-specific stress remark. Te…

sources.quote: O fator demarcativo do lexema é, portanto, o peso silábico, uma vez que uma sílaba pesada caracteriza sempre o final de um lexema, ao passo que uma sílaba leve caracteriza sempre a primeira sílaba de um lexema dissílabo.
